---
title: "Generator"
subtitle: "The families -C/-D/-E/-W, the scale options, and the instances they build"
---

Without `-d`, `zeno` builds the instance with the generating functions of the 2016 solvers, from
the options `-n -t -p -C -D -E -W -r -j -k -l -m -x -y`
([command line](../solver/cli.qmd#instance-options)). Every option means what its name says:
`-C` sets the **costs**, `-D` the **durations**, `-E` the **$C_I$-side** and `-W` the
**$C_G$-side** durations. The construction is `legacy::buildInstance`
(`src/zeno/legacy_input.cpp`). The 2016 solvers read the same options differently; see
[2016 and paper instances](#paper).

## Generating functions

`-C`, `-D`, `-E` and `-W` each take a code:

| Code | Function $f(k)$ | Name in the suites |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $\ln k$ | `log` |
| 2 | $\sqrt k$ | `sqrt` |
| 3 (default) | $k$ | `linear`, identity |
| 4 | $2^k$ | `pow2` |
| 5 | $5\lfloor k/2 \rfloor + 0.1\,(k \bmod 2)$ | `staircase`, the "(5/2)$i$" family |

Any other code falls back to the identity, as in 2016. The argument $k$ is truncated to an unsigned
integer before $f$ is applied, as the 2016 functions took `unsigned`.

## Construction

For cities $i = 1, \dots, n$, with $r$ = `-r`, $(j, k)$ = `-j -k`, $(l, m)$ = `-l -m` and $(x, y)$ =
`-x -y` (defaults $r = 1$, $j = l = x = 1$, $k = m = y = 0$):

1. Costs on increasing arguments, durations on **decreasing** ones:
   $$c_i = x\,f_C(\lfloor j\,i + k \rfloor) + y, \qquad d_i = x\,f_D(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y.$$
   With `-E` and `-W` (both needed; `-D` is then ignored) the instance is non-symmetric:
   $$d_i = x\,f_E(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y, \qquad \bar d_i = x\,f_W(\lfloor l\,(n+1-i) + m \rfloor) + y.$$
   Otherwise $\bar d = d$.
2. Every value is multiplied by $r$ and truncated toward zero: $v \leftarrow \operatorname{trunc}(r\,v)$.
   `-r 100` keeps slowly growing functions such as $\ln$ from collapsing onto a few integers.

With increasing functions, the first city is the slowest and the cheapest: faster cities cost
more, which is what makes the front non-trivial. The order of the cities does not matter to the
front.

## Examples

These are the outputs of `zeno generate` (durations, then costs; 3 lines when non-symmetric):

| Options | Instance |
|---|---|
| `-n 4` (defaults, linear) | $d = (4, 3, 2, 1)$, $c = (1, 2, 3, 4)$ |
| `-n 4 -C 2 -D 2 -r 10` | $d = (20, 17, 14, 10)$, $c = (10, 14, 17, 20)$ |
| `-n 10 -D 1 -r 100` | $d = (230, 219, 207, 194, 179, 160, 138, 109, 69, 0)$, $c = (100, 200, \dots, 1000)$ |
| `-n 10 -D 1` | $d = (2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0)$, $c = (1, 2, \dots, 10)$ |
| `-n 4 -E 3 -W 2 -r 10` | $d = (40, 30, 20, 10)$, $\bar d = (20, 17, 14, 10)$, $c = (10, 20, 30, 40)$ |

Zero values are allowed and do occur: $\ln 1 = 0$, so the log family has a city of duration or
cost 0.

## 2016 and paper instances {#paper}

The 2016 solvers, and the papers' instances, used the same generating functions, then exchanged
the duration and cost vectors (and reversed the $C_G$-side durations) whenever the first duration
exceeded the second. Their generator computes durations on decreasing arguments, so for an
increasing function this always happened, unless truncation made the first two durations equal.
`zeno` does not do this. To rebuild a 2016 instance, translate its options:

| 2016 / paper | `zeno` |
|---|---|
| `-C a -D b` | `-C b -D a`, and `-j -k` exchanged with `-l -m` |
| `-C c -E a -W b` | `-C a -E c -W b` |
| `-d FILE` with $d_1 > d_2$ | a file with the lines exchanged: costs, then durations (3 lines: costs, the $C_G$-side line reversed, the $C_I$-side line) |

`-n -t -p -r -x -y` are unchanged. Translated options build the 2016 instance with its cities in
the reverse order, which leaves the front unchanged; a translated data file builds it exactly. Two
cases need care:

- **No swap in 2016.** If the 2016 run did not swap, keep its options as they are. To tell, run
  `zeno generate` with the 2016 options: the 2016 solver swapped exactly when the first duration it
  prints exceeds the second. For example `-n 10 -D 1` (with `-r 1`) starts $d = (2, 2, \dots)$, so
  the 2016 solver did not swap it, while `-n 10 -D 1 -r 100` starts $d = (230, 219, \dots)$ and was
  swapped.
- **Non-symmetric scales.** `zeno` scales both duration sides with `-l -m`. The `-E`/`-W`
  translation is exact when the 2016 instance had the same `-j -k` as `-l -m`, in particular at the
  defaults. Otherwise write the 2016 instance as a data file.

With these rules, a 2016 instance whose two duration functions coincided after the swap, such as
`-C 3 -E 1 -W 3`, was in fact symmetric; its translation `-C 1 -E 3 -W 3` is symmetric too.

The committed suites are written in the current meaning. When the swap was removed, two benchmark
instances (`families/log-linear` and `families/sqrt-linear`) and six golden instances were
rewritten this way, and every front stayed the same. The golden names keep their 2016 flags: the
golden `n3t5p2-C1D4r10` runs `-n 3 -t 5 -p 2 -r 10 -C 4 -D 1` (header of
`tests/golden/instances.txt`).

## The families in the suites

The `families` suite runs every family on $n = 10$, $t = 8$, $p = 3$
([suites](suites.qmd#suite-families)): `linear` (`-C 3 -D 3`), `log` (`-C 1 -D 1 -r 100`), `sqrt`
(`-C 2 -D 2 -r 100`), `pow2` (`-C 4 -D 4`), `staircase` (`-C 5 -D 5 -r 10`), and the mixed
`log-linear` (logarithmic durations and linear costs, `-C 3 -D 1 -r 100`) and `sqrt-linear`
(`-C 3 -D 2 -r 100`). The default family is the only one with a closed-form front
([known fronts](known-fronts.qmd)). The others need the general algorithm, and on them the 2016
greedy can miss points.

Every instance the generator builds without `-E`/`-W` is symmetric, and every PDDL problem `zeno`
writes from it satisfies (A1), so its front is exact.
